title: Thanksgiving's strange contradiction: More stuff, less gratitude

title: How to Preach to Workers
summary: The New Testament offers two paradigms for how preachers can consider workers in their teaching.
summary_zh: 我还记得我第一次听到关于上帝设计工作的布道。 科林·史密斯牧师参加了一系列通过"十诫"的工作,他来到了安息日的第四个指挥. 我期待听到关于休息的有挑战性的话。 所以我很惊讶,当他用 他的布道的前半部分 谈论工作。
title_zh: 如何向工人传福音
content: I still remember the first time I heard a sermon on God’s design for work. Pastor Colin Smith was in a series working through the Ten Commandments, and he’d come to the fourth command about the Sabbath. I was expecting to hear challenging words about rest. So I was surprised when he spent the first half of his sermon talking about work. Because he’s a good exegetical preacher, Smith reminded us to pay attention to the part of the passage we might overlook: “Six days you shall labor, and do all your work . . .” (Ex. 20:9). For 16 minutes, Smith preached about God’s design for work. He explained how God modeled work in creation, crafting and making our world like a builder, engineer, and artist. And since humans were created in the likeness of this God, our labors are a significant part of what it means to represent him in the world. Then he started naming regular kinds of work—such as the school crossing guard who creates a zone of safety and protection for children. He shared example after example, even naming those who are were unemployed and looking for work as engaging in a form of dignified labor. They can please God as they trust him to provide and remain diligent to seek out what’s next. At the time, I was working a summer landscaping job between semesters at seminary. I took the job because it was necessary, not because I found it personally fulfilling or spiritually significant. I’d been subconsciously wanting to be done with mowing lawns and picking weeds so I could get back to the important work of studying Scripture. But God used Smith’s sermon to reorient my ordinary labor. Preaching with workers in mind is vital to shepherding a congregation. It reminds church members that work is a primary context for discipleship and helps them work out the implications of God’s Word where they spend a large portion of their time. The New Testament gives two paradigms for how preachers can consider workers in their teaching. Work as an Illustration of the Kingdom As the eternal, perfect Son of God, Jesus isn’t only Savior and Lord but also the most brilliant teacher the world has ever heard. Therefore, as preachers, we take his pedagogy seriously even as we learn his precepts and mimic his practices. Jesus often proclaims the good news by igniting people’s imaginations and explaining eternal truths in concrete realities, including the body (Matt. 6:22; 7:3–5; 24:7–8), nature (Matt. 6:28–29; Mark 11:23; Luke 17:6), and food (Matt. 13:33; John 6:35, 53–56). But Jesus’s most consistent metaphor for the truths of the kingdom is work and workers. Klaus Issler’s survey reveals that of the 37 parables in the Synoptic Gospels, 32 reference work or workers, representing 22 different work roles. In 25 of the parables, work is a main part of the storyline. Here are examples: The farmer sows the seed (Matt. 13). The faithful manager gives the servants of the household food at the proper time (Luke 12:42). Even an unjust judge will give a persistent widow justice (18:1–8). The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). A king going into battle should take counsel to see if he’s strong enough before he a ttacks (Luke 14:31). When Jesus describes what it meant to follow him and live in his kingdom, why does he use the ordinary language of work and workers? First, God’s self-disclosure is often wrapped in the language of work. For instance, he’s portrayed as a composer and performer (Deut. 31:19), a tentmaker (Job 9:8), a garment maker and dresser (29:14), a shepherd (Ps. 23:1–4), a builder (Prov. 8:27–31), a metalworker (Isa. 1:24–26), a potter (31:9), and a farmer (Hos. 10:11). If God is the original worker, it makes sense that the whole realm of work can teach us his ways. If God is the original worker, it makes sense that the whole realm of work can teach us his ways. Second, Jesus likely spent nearly six times as many years as a regular worker than he did in his public ministry—probably as a stonemason, either running a small family business or working as a day laborer. Wouldn’t it make sense that 17 or 18 years of regular work would inform the language of his teaching? It isn’t a coincidence that Jesus summarizes the implications of his teaching with the image of two builders: one who built on a sturdy foundation and one who built on sand (Matt. 7:24–27). Jesus knows by experience the ramifications of choosing the wrong foundation. So that’s the mental model he gives us to understand ways we can respond to his teaching. From Jesus to the Pulpit Jesus isn’t alone in using work as an illustration of the kingdom. Paul calls himself an expert builder who lays a foundation others build on (1 Cor. 3:10). He also instructs Timothy to meditate on the work of soldiers, athletes, and farmers to learn what it means to be a faithful pastor in Ephesus (2 Tim. 2:3–7). James too, in his final climactic call to wait for the Lord’s return, tells us to consider farmers who patiently wait for autumn and spring rains (James 5:7–8). When the New Testament writers explain what it means to walk with God, they regularly use examples from ordinary work. What might this mean for preachers today? As we explain the principles of God’s kingdom, how could we illustrate gospel truths with the work of baristas, software developers, accountants, realtors, or construction workers? How are God’s ways like a home inspector or a pilot? How is following him like the work of a middle manager or a plumber? To teach like Jesus and the writers of the epistles is to search out and proclaim the truth of the kingdom in the language of regular work. Along with making our teaching vivid, this dignifies people—in a unique way, their daily work is a picture of how God is at work in the world, and we can better understand who he is and what he calls us to if we look closely at the labor of his image-bearers. Work as an Application of the Gospel While Jesus primarily uses work to illustrate the kingdom, other New Testament writers mention work as a direct application of embracing the gospel. And even though the epistles aren’t sermons, they demonstrate how the apostles applied the gospel to common pastoral and contextual issues. For instance, Paul encourages the Corinthians, who have just been told of the wonders of the resurrection body, to know that their labor in the Lord isn’t in vain (1 Cor. 15:58). In a culture of persistent stealing, the Ephesians are called to do work that produces something good, so they’ll be able to give to those in need (Eph. 4:28). Bondservants with little power or agency are told to work diligently (6:5–9), knowing they’ll receive an inheritance as their reward and that their true Master is God himself (Col. 3:23–24). Those in Thessalonica who deem it more spiritual to constantly await God’s return without worrying about ordinary work are commanded to lead quiet lives, working with their hands (1 Thess. 4:11–12). James confronts boastful business leaders, saying they need to have a more God-dependent outlook (James 4:13–16) and that rich landowners who aren’t paying their workers can expect judgment (5:1–6). And Paul calls Philemon to envision a new working relationship with Onesimus, based not on power or status but on brotherly love and affection (Philem. 1:10–16). After articulating the gospel, the epistle writers consistently model that its application must be made clearly and contextually to people’s work. This suggests work should be a top-tier pastoral concern, with implications for the church’s regular teaching ministry. Work should be a top-tier pastoral concern, with implications for the church’s regular teaching ministry. Preaching to workers is a lifelong endeavor. Modeled by Jesus, the New Testament authors, and countless preachers throughout church history, in many times and in many places, the practice is rooted in pastoral curiosity and a desire to shepherd the people of God in their ordinary lives. 由于他是一个优秀的传教士,史密斯提醒我们注意我们可能忽略的那段话:"六天你必须努力,并做你所有的工作."(前20:9). 16分钟后,史密斯宣扬了"上帝"的工作设计. 他解释了上帝如何塑造我们的世界 像一个建筑师、工程师和艺术家
由于人类是在这个神的相似之处创造的, 我们的劳动是在世界中代表他的意义的重要部分. 然后,他开始点名定期工作——例如为孩子创造安全和保护区的校外警卫。

它提醒教会成员,工作是门徒活动的主要背景,并帮助他们在他们花费一大部分时间的地方研究出"上帝之言"的影响. 新约为传道者如何在教学中考虑工人给出了两种范式.
作为王国的启示 作为永恒而完美的上帝之子,耶稣不仅是救世主和上帝,而且是全世界听过的最有才华的老师。 因此,作为传道者,我们在学习他的戒律并模仿他的做法时,也认真对待他的教学方法.
耶稣经常通过点燃人们的想象力和在具体现实中解释永恒的真理来宣布好消息,包括身体(Matt. 6:22;7:3–5;24:7–8),自然(Matt. 6:28–29;Mark 11:23;Luke 17:6)和食物(Matt. 13:33;John 6:35,53–56). 但耶稣对王国真理最一致的比喻是工作和工人.

首先,上帝的自我披露常常被工作语言所包裹. 例如,他被描绘成作曲家和表演者(德国:31:19)、帐篷匠(约旦:9:8)、制衣和梳妆师(29:14)、牧羊人(Ps:23:1-4)、建筑师(Prov:8:27-31)、金属工人(Isa:1:24-26)、锅炉工(31:9)和农民(Hos:10:11)。

从耶稣到雕塑耶稣, 保罗自称是一位专家建筑师,他为他人在(1 Cor. 他还指示蒂莫西沉思士兵,运动员和农民的工作,学习在以弗所做忠实牧师的意义(2 Tim. 2:3-7).
詹姆斯在最后的高潮召唤中也要求我们等待主的归来,要求我们考虑耐心地等待秋天和春雨(詹姆斯:7–8)的农民. 当"新约"作家解释"与神同行"的意义时,他们经常使用从平凡作品中取出的例子. 这对今天的传教士意味着什么?
当我们解释上帝王国的原则时,我们如何用律师、软件开发者、会计师、房地产商或建筑工人的工作来说明福音真理呢? 如何是上帝的方式 像一个家庭巡视员或飞行员? 如何是跟随他 像一个中层经理或水管工的工作?
像耶稣和史诗作家一样教书,就是用正作的语言去探寻并宣告王国的真理. 除了让我们的教学生动地进行外,这还使人们深受尊重——以独特的方式,他们的日常工作是描绘出上帝如何在世界上工作,如果我们仔细观察他的形象持有者的工作,我们就能更好地了解他是谁,以及他叫我们做什么。
工作是福音书的应用 虽然耶稣主要用活来说明王国,但其他"新约"的作者提到工作是接受福音书的直接应用. 也说明使徒们如何将福音运用于常见的牧业和背景问题。
例如,保罗鼓励刚刚被告知复活生灵之奇的科林斯人知道他们在主的劳动并非白费一分(第15:58节)。 在持续偷盗的文化中,以弗所人被要求从事能产生好东西的工作,这样他们就能把工作交给有需要的人(Eph.4:28)。
他们知道自己会得到一笔遗产作为报酬,而且他们真正的主人是上帝本人(Col. 3:23-24)。 在特萨洛尼察,那些认为在不担心普通工作的情况下不断等待上帝的归来更具有精神的人奉命过上平和的生活,用双手工作(1 Thess. 4:11-12).
詹姆斯面对自夸的商界领袖,说他们需要有一个更依赖上帝的前景(詹姆斯4:13-16),而不支付工人工资的富地主可以期待判断(5:1-6). 保罗呼吁菲莱蒙设想与Onesimus建立新的工作关系,这种关系不是基于权力或地位,而是基于兄弟般的爱和亲情(Philem. 1:10-16)。

content: Paul’s plea to Timothy to bring him his cloak and his books is a powerful reminder of how important books have been throughout Christian history (2 Tim. 4:13). Though death seemed near, Paul still longed to study. Good books can strengthen the soul. Amid the flood of new works published every year, it can be hard to find the sorts of books you would want with you on death row. The Gospel Coalition’s editorial team works hard to identify the best evangelical books published each year. This announcement is the culmination of months of hard work by a big team of book lovers. We receive nominations from publishers in 11 categories. Then our editors work together to recommend finalists in each category. Finally, a panel of judges reads each one carefully before casting their votes. The books are evaluated for the way they offer gospel-centered argument and application; include faithful and foundational use of Scripture, both Old Testament and New Testament; foster spiritual discernment of contemporary trials and trends; and encourage efforts to unite and renew the church. The result is a list of 22 books we recommend as helpful resources for the church and for individual believers. We hope you enjoy and are edified by them. You can find the books in a curated list at a discount in TGC’s online bookstore . Additionally, at the bottom of this article, you’ll find books that TGC has published this year, which were ineligible for our book awards. Congratulations to the winners of the 2026 TGC Book Awards. Andrew Spencer Books Editor Popular Theology Dane Ortlund, Finally Home: The Christian Hope of Heaven (Crossway) This world is beautiful, but it’s broken. Its sorrows remind us that something is terribly wrong; its joys whisper that something unimaginably better is coming. In Finally Home , Dane Ortlund turns our gaze toward that glorious future. With theological depth and the tenderness of a pastor who knows how to speak to weary souls, he brings the hope of heaven down to earth, speaking directly to the sorrows and struggles of everyday life. Here’s a book for Christians who need reminding that suffering will not have the last word, that Jesus will make all things new, and that the best is gloriously yet to come. You’ll finish these pages longing for home—and loving the Savior who will welcome you there. Award of Distinction Brett McCracken, The Wisdom of Sleep: How Rest Reveals God’s Truth and Revives Weary Souls (Zondervan) What if one of the most spiritual things you could do tonight is close your eyes and go to sleep? In The Wisdom of Sleep , Brett McCracken takes an activity we spend roughly a third of our lives doing and reveals its surprising theological significance. Pushing back against our culture’s relentless obsession with productivity, he draws on Scripture, science, and cultural insight to show that sleep isn’t a necessary evil or a strategy for getting more done. It’s a gift from God; a nightly reminder that we’re creatures, not the Creator; and a signpost pointing toward our eternal rest in Christ. Refreshingly practical and richly biblical, this book will leave you more grateful for the gift of sleep and more amazed by the God who never slumbers. Judges: Joshua Chatman, Juan Sánchez, Matt Smethurst, Laura Spaulding Ministry Tony Payne , Let the Word Dwell Richly: The Vital Power of the One-Another Word (Matthias Media) Evangelicals remain steadfastly committed to the ministry of God’s Word. And in our Reformed tradition, the sermon—public proclamation of the Word—rightfully takes center stage in our worship. Yet in our emphasis on expositional preaching, have we overlooked the Word ministry God gives to every Christian? Have we neglected the one-another word the New Testament writers repeatedly commend? Those are the questions Tony Payne answers with biblical clarity and practical insight in this follow-up to his classic with Colin Marshall, The Trellis and the Vine . Building on his own exegetical and theological research, Payne unpacks the complementary roles public proclamation and private exhortation play in a healthy local church. In preaching, pastors declare forth God’s Word with conviction, applying Scripture broadly to the whole church. Yet the New Testament also assumes all believers will speak words of wisdom to one another, applying eternal truth to specific life situations. Payne’s point is that if we want to see our churches mature, we must cultivate environments where both kinds of speaking thrive. Every pastor, group leader, and Sunday school teacher will benefit from thoughtful reflection on the ideas Payne presents in Let the Word Dwell Richly . Award of Distinction Timothy St. John, After Church Hurt: Healing in the Care of the Good Shepherd (New Growth) In our therapeutic age, the idea of church hurt is pervasive, and it can feel confusing and even threatening for church leaders. We all—from pastors to members—desperately need a clear understanding of church hurt. And perhaps more, we need a pathway toward preventing it and healing from it. In After Church Hurt , Timothy St. John gives church leaders a gospel-rich and scripturally grounded tool for defining church hurt and navigating through it. Whether you’ve been hurt by the church or are striving to be the kind of leader who does no harm, St. John will help you understand church hurt biblically, learn how to embrace God’s grace, and then move toward church unity without minimizing pain or excusing abuse. This book is highly practical and culturally redemptive. We hope many in the church will read it. Judges: Brandon Cooper, Jared Kennedy, Walt Nilsson, Jen Oshman Christian Living Jen Wilkin, Dust to Dust: Aging Wisely in an Anti-Aging World (Crossway) We’re regularly bombarded with images and messages that tell us our worth is found in how we look and that aging is something to be feared. In Dust to Dust , Jen Wilkin tells us the true story of aging. She helps readers see the stages of life as a chiasm—a mirrored journey that begins and ends with the need for dignity and dependence. In an age where the church is on the cusp of experiencing demographic inversion, we need a stronger theology of aging and a clearer understanding of our Christian duty to love our aging neighbor as ourselves. Wilkin offers biblically robust arguments for seeing and valuing people through the end of life, whether in the context of our biological families or in the broader church family. In this, she pushes against the individualistic, youth-obsessed status quo. Most importantly, Dust to Dust asks readers to ponder their own presuppositions about what makes life meaningful. Spoiler alert: It’s not a fresh-looking face, the absence of gray hair, or the abundance of lean muscle. Wilkin clearly explains that growing in Christlike character and wisdom, even as our bodies decay, is a witness to the watching world of our hope in heaven. Award of Distinction William P. Smith, You Are Not Alone: How God Solves Our Isolation and Loneliness (P&R) In a world of unprecedented connectivity, it seems odd to think of ourselves as alone. Yet nearly everyone in today’s society experiences some level of isolation and loneliness. It’s par for the course in a digital age where we stare at screens instead of faces and live increasingly individualistic lives. In You Are Not Alone , William P. Smith insightfully diagnoses the varying facets of aloneness in modern society, demonstrating that the feeling of being alone isn’t merely about physical separation. Smith identifies and unpacks root issues that cause people to avoid relationships, leave the church, and drift further into a solitary life. Ultimately, Smith presents the overarching gospel story as both the explanation for and the solution to our struggles with isolation and loneliness. When we understand that we’re seen, known, and loved by God, we can move toward community and embrace the relationships we were created for from a deep sense of acceptance i

保罗恳求蒂莫西将他的斗篷和书籍带给他,这有力地提醒人们在整个基督教历史(2 Tim. 4: 13)中书的重要性. 虽然死亡似乎接近,但保罗仍然渴望学习. 好书能加强灵魂. 在每年出版的一大批新作中, 很难找到在死囚牢里你想要的书。
福音书联盟的编辑团队努力确定每年出版的最好的福音书. 这个公告是一大批书迷数月来辛勤工作的高潮. 我们收到11类出版社的提名。 然后,我们的编辑们合作推荐每个类别的入围者。
最后,一个法官小组在投票前仔细阅读每个法官。 对这些书的评价是它们提供以福音为中心的论据和应用的方式;包括忠实和基础地使用《圣经》,包括《旧约》和《新约》;培养对当代试验和趋势的精神认知;鼓励努力团结并更新教会。
结果是我们推荐的22本书的清单,作为教会和个别信徒的有用资源。 我们希望你们享受并被他们吃上。 在TGC网上书店, 此外,在文章的底部,你会发现TGC今年出版的书籍,这些书籍没有资格获得我们的书奖。
祝贺2026TGC图书奖获奖者. Andrew Spencer Books 编辑 大众神学 Dane Ortlund, 最后出道: 基督教的天堂希望 (克罗斯韦) 这个世界是美丽的, 它的悲痛提醒我们,有些事情是极其错误的;它的喜悦悄悄地说,有些事情即将来临,这是不可想象的。
Dane Ortlund将我们的目光转向辉煌的未来。 凭借神学的深度和一位会向疲惫的灵魂说话的牧师的温柔,他把天堂的希望带到了地上,直接对日常生活的悲伤和斗争说话.
这是一本供基督徒阅读的书, 他们需要提醒人们, 苦难不会是最后一句话, 耶稣会让万事皆新, 你会完成这些渴望回家的页面,
Brett McCracken杰出奖 " 睡眠的智慧:上帝的真理和疲劳的复兴如何安息 " (Zondervan) 如果你今晚能做的最有精神的事情之一 就是闭上眼睛去睡觉呢? 在"睡眠之智慧"中,布雷特·麦克拉肯(Brett McCracken)采取一项活动,我们花了我们生命的大约三分之一时间来做,并揭示出其惊人的神学意义.
他利用圣经、科学和文化洞察力来表明睡眠不是必然的罪恶, 这是来自上帝的礼物;夜以继夜地提醒我们,我们是生物,不是造物主;以及指向我们在基督中永恒安息的路标。
这本书会令你更感激 睡眠的天赋 更惊讶于从未入睡的上帝 法官:约书亚·查特曼、胡安·桑切斯、马特·斯梅特赫斯特、劳拉·斯波丁部长托尼·佩恩、让《言语之井》富足: " 一个又一个言语(Matthias Media)的重要力量 " 福音派人士仍然坚定致力于神语之道。
在我们改革后的传统中,布道——公开宣示言语——恰好在我们礼拜中占据了中心位置。 然而,在我们强调讲解时,我们是否忽略了上帝给予每个基督徒的言语? 我们是否忽视了"新约"作家反复称赞的又一个词?
这些是托尼·佩恩在跟科林·马歇尔(Colin Marshall),"The Trellis"(The Trellis)和"葡萄"(Vine)的经典续作中,以圣经的清晰和切实的见解回答的问题. 佩恩在自己的开天辟地和神学研究的基础上,整理了在健康的地方教会中公开宣布和私下劝告的辅助作用.
在传道中,牧师们坚信地宣布真主的话语,将《圣经》广泛应用于整个教会。 然而"新约"也假定所有信徒都会互相说出智慧的话来,将永恒的真理运用到特定的生活状况. Payne的观点是,如果我们想让我们的教堂成熟,我们必须培育两种语言都兴旺的环境。
每个牧师、团体领袖和星期日的学校老师, Timothy St. John杰出奖,《教堂受创后:在善牧人照料下康复》(新成长) 在我们的治疗时代,教会伤害的想法是普遍存在的,它会感到困惑甚至威胁教会领袖.
我们——从牧师到成员——都迫切需要明确了解教会遭受的伤害。 也许,我们更需要一条路径 来预防它和治愈它。 在"Church Hurt"中,蒂莫西·圣约翰(Timothy St.
圣约翰会帮助你理解教会的伤害, 学习如何接受上帝的恩惠, 然后走向教会团结, 而不减少痛苦或免责。 这本书具有高度实用性和文化上的"红色"发作. 我们希望教会里很多人会读到它.
法官: Brandon Cooper、Jared Kennedy、Walt Nilsson、Jen Oshman Christian Living Jen Wilkin、 " 从尘到尘:在反老龄化世界中明智地老去 " (十字路口) 我们经常被那些告诉我们价值的图像和信息所轰炸, 在"尘至尘"中,仁·威尔金讲述了老化的真实故事.
她帮助读者将人生的各个阶段视为一个奇观——一个以尊严和依赖的需要为起点和终点的镜像之旅。 在教会正面临人口倒置的时代,我们需要一个更强烈的老化神学,需要更清楚地理解我们的基督教义务,爱我们的老邻居,就像我们自己一样。
威尔金为人们通过生命的终结,无论是在我们的生物家庭还是在更广泛的教会家庭中,来看待和重视他们提供了具有圣经意义的有力论据。 在此她推倒了个人主义的,青春主义的现状. 最重要的是,"尘到尘"要求读者思考他们自己的预想是什么让生命有意义.
破坏者警告:这不是一张新相貌,没有灰色发型,或者有丰富的瘦肌肉。 威尔金清楚地解释,在基督般的性格和智慧中成长,即使我们的身体已经衰败,也见证了我们天堂所希望的观察世界. (原始内容存档于2018-10-21). Award of Distriction William P.
Smith, You Are not Alone: 在一个前所未有的互联互通世界中,上帝如何解决我们的孤立和孤独(P&R), 把我们自己视为孤独似乎很奇怪. 然而,今天的社会中几乎每个人都会经历某种程度的孤立和孤独。 在数码时代, 看着屏幕而不是相貌,
威廉·P·史密斯(William P. Smith)在《你并非孤独》中深刻地分析了现代社会中孤独性的不同方面, 史密斯识别并解开导致人们回避关系,离开教堂并更进一步地漂入孤独生活的根源问题.
最终,史密斯提出了最重要的福音故事,作为解释和解决我们与孤立和孤独的斗争。 当我们明白我们被上帝所看见、认识和喜爱时, 我们可以走向社区, 拥抱我们从深刻的接受感 创造出来的关系

summary: Don’t wait for the perfect time. Trust the Lord, open the doors, and watch him bless his people.

title_zh: 晚间崇拜的文化塑造力
content: Recently, a friend asked me how things were going at the church where I serve. As I reflected on his question, I was overwhelmed with gratitude. The Lord has been astonishingly kind to our congregation over the past several years. We’ve become healthier, more unified, and more joyful. Then my friend asked a second question: “What changed?” Like many young churches, our early years included growing pains. We loved one another, but not always patiently. We were starting to believe the right truths, but we were still learning to put those truths into action. I thought of several possible answers: faithful elders, growing families, or the cumulative effect of years of expository preaching. Yet as I contemplated, I realized most of the growth in our congregation started with one small decision. Five years ago, our church began gathering at the close of each Lord’s Day for evening worship. Evening worship isn’t a magic formula for church growth or maturity. Christ alone builds his church, but he does use means. I’m convinced that gathering a second time each Lord’s Day has become one of the most significant means by which Christ has shaped the culture of our congregation. Tyranny of the ‘Perfect Time’ When we planted the church in 2013, we began with Sunday school and morning worship. I always hoped we’d eventually add an evening service, but it never seemed to be a good time. Ministry was demanding, other Sunday evening activities filled the calendar, and I worried about whether anyone would even show up. We were waiting for a perfect season that never arrived. None of my reasons for waiting was foolish, but five years later, I can say without hesitation that the Lord has done exceeding, abundantly beyond all we asked or imagined through evening worship. Here are four ways restoring evening worship has shaped our church’s culture. 1. Double Portion of the Means of Grace The most obvious blessing of evening worship is wonderfully simple: It gives our congregation another opportunity each Lord’s Day to gather around the ordinary means of grace. We gather to hear God’s Word read and preached, to pray, to sing his praises, and to enjoy the fellowship of his people. Taken individually, none of these things seems particularly impressive. We’ve become healthier, more unified, and more joyful. When we gather a second time, we aren’t inventing a new program; we’re doubling down on the same apostolic diet that sustained the early church: the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and the prayers (Acts 2:42). Those means of grace didn’t expire with the book of Acts; they’re still our Lord’s chosen means for growing his church (v. 47). Often, the conversation about whether to add an evening service begins with the inevitable question: “Does God require evening worship?” While I understand the nature of the question, we’d do better to have the perspective that evening worship isn’t another box to check or a legalistic obligation to bear. It’s an invitation to feast on the grace God delights to give. 2. Sweet, Unhurried Fellowship Evening worship has brought an unexpectedly sweet blessing: It has knitted our church family more tightly together. Sunday evenings have become a space where relationships are genuinely cultivated and deepened. When people gather only on Sunday morning, there’s an understandable urgency. Families often hurriedly arrive just before the prelude and leave soon after the postlude. Conversations are necessarily brief—our members have children to collect, lunches to prepare, and the looming reality of the workweek ahead. Evening worship changes the pace of church life. People tend to arrive earlier and linger longer. Families invite one another over for a meal between services. Friendships that might have taken years to develop in a morning lobby blossom over a casual Sunday evening dinner. Elders have spontaneous shepherding conversations that could never have been scheduled. Over time, we’ve seen these ordinary interactions produce extraordinary fruit. Evening worship has strengthened the communion of the saints, turning the biblical command to “stir up one another to love and good works” from a Sunday morning rush into a Sunday evening reality (Heb. 10:24–25). 3. Reclaiming the Whole Lord’s Day Another blessing of evening worship is the hardest to measure: It has slowly but surely reshaped our weekly habits. By bookending the Sabbath with worship, we’ve seen a cultural transformation in our church from functionally celebrating “the Lord’s Morning” to truly honoring “the Lord’s Day.” Along the way, Sundays have stopped feeling like a brief interruption to our weekend and have become the center around which the rest of our week is ordered. The hours between worship services are no longer time to go our own way before Monday arrives. Instead, the afternoon has become a haven for rest, hospitality, reading, and fellowship. We’re learning what the prophet Isaiah meant when he called the Sabbath a “delight” and the holy day of the Lord “honorable” (Isa. 58:13). I’m particularly excited for the ways this will shape the children of our church for years to come. They’re growing up learning that the Lord’s Day belongs to the Lord, and that worship isn’t something we squeeze into a busy schedule but the reality around which we gladly order our lives. 4. Joy of Costly Worship Gathering on Sunday evening means setting aside other good things—an afternoon of recreation, extra sleep, or the comfort of staying in our pajamas. In a culture that prizes convenience and leisure above all else, making the effort to gather a second time declares to our souls and to our world what we value most. Worship is sacrificial by nature, and therefore it becomes a test for our own hearts to determine if Christ is worthy of our first love. When we offer him only the brief, convenient scraps of our weekend, we flirt with the attitude of ancient Israel, who sniffed at God’s altar and called his worship wearisome (Mal. 1:13). Evening worship offers a corrective. King David understood this principle when he refused to offer burnt offerings to the Lord that “cost [him] nothing” (2 Sam. 24:24). Genuine worship always requires laying aside lesser loves because Christ is worthy of our first love. The cost of evening worship isn’t something churches should apologize for. Every Lord’s Day, our people quietly declare—to our children, to one another, and to our own anxious hearts—that Jesus Christ is worth rearranging our lives for. Members, Don’t Wait If you belong to a church that offers evening worship but you haven’t yet made it a part of your weekly practice, let me encourage you: Start this Sunday. Don’t wait until your schedule clears up or your kids get a little older. Dive into the deep end of the Lord’s Day. You’ll find that the initial sacrifice of your Sunday evening is swallowed up by the unparalleled delight of being with God’s people. Pastors, Don’t Wait Since seeing these blessings, I’ve spoken with many pastors who tell me, “We agree evening worship is good, but this just isn’t the right season for our church.” Genuine worship always requires laying aside lesser loves because Christ is worthy of our first love. I understand that hesitation because I lived it. Ministry is exhausting. We’re already stretched by obligations. But Christ hasn’t promised to build his church through perfect circumstances; he has promised to bless his appointed means. If your church is considering gathering for Lord’s Day evening worship, don’t feel it must be elaborate. Begin simply. Preach the Word. Pray. Sing. Gather God’s people once more before the sun sets, and trust Christ to do what he has always done through ordinary faithfulness. Trust the Lord and Open the Door If I could go back and give my younger, church-planting self one piece of advice, it would be this: Don’t wait for the perfect time. Trust the Lord, open the doors, and watch him bless his people. The fruit will
content_zh:
最近,一个朋友问我,我所在的教堂的情况如何。 我在思考他的问题时感到十分感激。 在过去的几年里,上帝对我们的教友们非常友好 我们变得更健康、更团结、更快乐。
然后,我的朋友问了第二个问题:“什么改变了?” 和许多年轻的教堂一样,我们的早年包括了不断增长的痛苦. 我们彼此相爱,但并不总是耐心的。 我们开始相信正确的真理,但我们仍在学习将这些真理付诸行动。
我想到了几个可能的答案:忠实的长者,不断成长的家庭,或者多年的通俗传道的累积效应. 然而,正如我所想的,我意识到,我们教友会的大部分增长始于一个小决定。 五年前,我们的教堂开始在每逢主节结束时聚集,进行晚间礼拜.
晚上的礼拜不是教会成长或成熟的法术。 基督独自建造他的教堂, 但他确实使用手段。 我深信,每个主日第二次聚会已经成为基督塑造我们教会文化的最重要手段之一。
" 完美时间 " 的暴风雨 2013年植入教堂后,从星期天的学校开始并进行晨祷. 我总是希望我们最终会增加晚间服务, 我担心是否有人会出现。 我们等待着一个从未到来的完美的季节。
我等待的理由都不愚蠢,但是五年后,我可以毫不犹豫地说,上帝已经超越了我们通过晚礼而要求或想象的一切。 以下是四种恢复晚间礼拜的方式, 1. 联合国
双相的恩惠手段 晚上崇拜最明显的祝福是极其简单的: 它使我们的会众再次有机会在每逢主日聚集在普通的恩惠手段周围。 我们聚集一堂,听取上帝的言辞,宣读并宣讲,祈祷,歌颂他,享受他所生人民的友谊.
从个别情况来看,这些事情似乎都不特别令人印象深刻。 我们变得更健康、更团结、更快乐。 当我们第二次聚会时, 我们并没有发明新的计划; 我们正用维持早期教会的同样背信弃义的饮食翻一番:使徒们的教诲、奖学金、断面包和祈祷(第2:42号法案)。
这些恩典并没有随着法令书而过期;它们仍然是我们的主选择的培养他教会的手段(v.47)。
有关是否增加晚间礼拜的谈话往往从一个不可避免的问题开始:“上帝需要晚间礼拜吗?” 虽然我理解问题的性质, 我们最好还是从这个角度来看待晚会礼拜, 以享受上帝赐予的恩惠。 2. 联合国
令人意外地祝福: 它使我们的教会家庭更加紧密地联系在一起。 星期天晚上已成为真正培育和加深关系的空间。 当人们只在星期天早上聚集时,

title: In the Darkness, Christmas Shines a Light
summary: The general revelation of God’s created order—darkness and light, night and day—primes every created thing to know they need light, a salvation from outside themselves.
summary_zh: 某些花朵 -- -- 日出花朵、罂粟和日出花朵, 空荡荡的街道 安静的房屋被搅动了 我们从休息转向工作,静态转向活动。 我们从休息转向工作,静态转向活动。 我们被太阳能所活化、生长和繁荣。 与神同为也.
title_zh: 在黑暗中，圣诞节照亮光明
content: Read For behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and thick darkness the peoples; but the LORD will arise upon you, and his glory will be seen upon you. And nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising. (Isa. 60:2–3) Reflect There’s something about a sunrise. It wakes the world. Unlike the jarring blare of an alarm clock, a sunrise quietly whispers “Wake, O sleeper” with the graceful love of a parent rubbing a sleeping child’s back. When the sun rises, the slumbering stir to life. We’ve just spent seven or eight hours dead to the world. Then the sunrise triggers in us what looks like a resurrection. We rise. Certain flowers—daisies, poppies, and the aptly named morning glories—open their blossoms at the sun’s rising. Little by little, empty streets fill and quiet houses stir. Drawn to the warmth and energy of the just-unveiled sun, we transition from rest to work, stillness to activity. Drawn to the warmth and energy of the just-unveiled sun, we transition from rest to work, stillness to activity. It’s not surprising that the sun is an oft-used metaphor for God. For he, too, resurrects the dead. He, too, is the Giver of life and growth. He, too, draws all things to himself—such as the trees, which by nature grow upward, toward the sun, their branches like arms raised in perpetual worship. This is the created order. All things were made to be drawn to and sustained by the sun. We were made to be alive insofar as we live, grow, and flourish by solar energy. So too with God. We’re in darkness and death without him. As he bestows his grace on us, we rise to new life. We’re able to grow. Like the sunflower blossom, which turns to follow the sun wherever it’s positioned in the sky, we’re created to look to the Lord, who “will arise upon [us], and his glory will be seen upon [us]” (Isa. 60:2). In a world of darkness, we ache for the light. We wait for the sunrise. All nations, all kings, all people share this in common. The horizon each of us looks to—the nature of the “new day” we await—may be different: A new job. A remodeled home. A regime change. But only the sunrise of Christ will eternally satisfy. His is “the true light, which gives light to everyone” (John 1:9). Isaiah’s prophecy was fulfilled in him. Only the sunrise of Christ will eternally satisfy. The general revelation of God’s created order—darkness and light, night and day—primes every created thing to know they need light, a salvation from outside themselves. The special revelation of Christ reveals a truer light than even the sun: the light that is our eternal life, the light the darkness will never overcome (v. 5), the light that will one day end night as we know it (Rev. 22:5). Respond How is God’s glory seen in your life? How are you reflecting his beauty? In contrast to those who dwell in darkness, how does your life reflect 1 Thessalonians 5:5: “You are all children of light, children of the day. We are not of the night or of the darkness”?

title: Editor’s Pick: Middle-Grade Books
summary: The best children’s literature does more than preach to us; it draws us into the story while pointing toward truth, goodness, and beauty.
summary_zh: 我还在读儿童书籍。 有时我会重读我小时候所欣赏的同一本书:纳尼亚纪事、伯特·布林的"巴恩"、"小不列颠"、"侦探"弗雷迪和"哈地男孩"。 有时,我读到一些新书 出来吸引我的注意力, 如"游牧地的老师" 或最新的绿色Ember系列。 我读我以前最爱的作品的经验 与成年人不同 我仍然喜欢那些更古老的故事,但我有时会想知道弗兰克和乔·哈迪在经历了这么多脑震荡之后的后些年表现如何.
title_zh: 编辑精选：中年级读物
content: I still read children’s books. Sometimes I reread the same books I enjoyed as a child: The Chronicles of Narnia , Bert Breen’s Barn , Little Britches , Freddy the Detective , and The Hardy Boys . Sometimes I read newer books that come out that catch my attention, like The Teacher of Nomad Land or the latest in the Green Ember series. My experience of reading my old favorites is different as an adult. I still enjoy the older stories, but I sometimes wonder how Frank and Joe Hardy fared in their later years after getting so many concussions. I often enjoy the new stories, though I’m certain I don’t experience them the same way the target audience does, which is a little like knowing Narnia exists and not getting to visit it again for a long time. In his book Make Believe: On Telling Stories to Children , Mac Barnett explains what makes for a good children’s novel: “The best children’s writers tell the truth in a way that is recognizable and authentic to children.” The key is truth and connection with the audience. C. S. Lewis said something similar in his essay “ On Three Ways of Writing for Children ” many years ago. Children’s books helped me process the world. I read a lot of junk as a child, but I read a lot of good books too. And the good books were the ones that helped me understand why I was feeling frustration over a teacher’s unfairness, resentment about a classmate’s teasing, or fear of the turmoil in the adult world that streamed at me through the radio and television. The best sorts of children’s literature teach us something. Barnett caused a kerfuffle when his little book came out because he declared that “94.7 percent of kids’ books are crud.” He had in his sights overtly didactic books, with the industrial complex of volumes telling kids to “be kind” ad nauseam in his crosshairs. Quality children’s literature does more than preach to us; it draws us into the story while pointing toward truth, goodness, and beauty. I’ve put together a list of middle-grade books (though Barnett dislikes that label) that have been published in the last year or so. I enjoyed them because they told a story well and I learned something about the truth along the way. 1. Jonathan Rogers, The Charlatan’s Boy (Rabbit Room Press, 2026) Most children’s literature is, in some sense, about identity. That’s a major theme in The Charlatan’s Boy , as Grady travels around Corenwald with Floyd, the man who found him as a baby. When townspeople stop believing in feechiefolk—the mysterious residents of Feechiefen Swamp—Grady can no longer make a living by pretending to be a feechie. Instead, Floyd puts him on display as the ugliest boy alive. Though I suspected where the story would end, I didn’t want to put the book down because I couldn’t tell what Grady and Floyd were going to do next. It’s simply a well-told story. But I also appreciated that the whole story subtly reminds readers that durable identity is received, not chosen. It’s the best sort of book that captures the imagination even as it points us toward truth. 2. S. D. Smith, The Lost Cause (Story Warren, 2026) The publication of a new Green Ember book was cause for celebration when my kids were younger. The saying “It will not be so in the Mended Wood” became part of our household vernacular shortly after we met Picket, Heather, and Helmer for the first time. And although my children are past the age where it’s cool to be interested in rabbits with swords, my publicity copies of Smith’s books mysteriously disappear from my to-be-read stack before I get to them. I love these stories because they make me long for goodness, truth, and beauty. In a culture of sarcasm and skepticism, Smith reminds us that virtues like hope, loyalty, and perseverance are worth striving for. The Lost Cause is the third book in a sequence within the world of Natalia. It’s not the best place to jump into the story; those new to the series would be well served by beginning with The Green Ember , or at least the first in this sequence, The Lost Key . If you’re building a home library for your middle-grade readers, the Green Ember series is a great place to start. 3. Ben Palpant, Brightwing Tales: Acorn’s Misadventure (Brightwing Books, 2026) I came across Palpant’s work with his nonfiction book, An Axe for the Frozen Sea , a series of interviews with Christian poets about beauty, wonder, and art. His Brightwing Tales are the sort of children’s stories you’d expect from someone who loves good poetry. The first volume in the series, Brightwing Tales: Mole’s Misadventure , weaves a narrative about Mr. Mole through episodic chapters. It includes ghost stories, a hungry cat, a quest for pie, and a beautiful love story. Some of the scenes Palpant describes are so poignantly beautiful they brought tears to my eyes. The world reminded me of Wind in the Willows and Winnie-the-Pooh even before I read the description on his website. This second volume, Brightwing Tales: Acorn’s Misadventure , has a stronger narrative arc as it recounts the unusual friendship between a mouse named Acorn and Bear (who is a bear). It’s a story of loss, of longing, and of redemption. This is the sort of book that can shape a child’s imagination, helping him or her to see the goodness of the world even when everything looks dark. I enjoyed reading it myself and look forward to reading it to grandchildren one day. 4. Kathryn Butler, Escape from Rome (Crossway, 2026) I read dozens of Choose Your Own Adventure stories as a kid. Many of them on the school bus. Those books let me find treasure, die at the hands of pirates, get lost in outer space, and rescue damsels in distress all in one afternoon. They were a long way from highbrow literature, but the series was fun. Butler has two Decide-as-You-Go Adventures in Crossway’s Lamplight series, which use a similar format. In Escape from Rome , a summer visit to a cousin ends up with a broken lamp, a time-traveling adventure, and choices that have consequences. Will you admit to breaking the lamp or try to shift the blame? Will you get stuck in ancient Rome or will you make it back to the present? Every decision leads down a different path, sometimes to unpredictable results. Part of the fun is trying to navigate through all the possible pathways. I enjoyed this book as a bit of nostalgia, but I know one young reader at church who absolutely loves the books for their own sakes. 5. Paul Cox, Martin Williams, and Joy Williams, John Calvin’s Illustrated Institutes: The Word of God (P&R, 2026) One of my concerns as a parent and a pastor is that we’re not effective at communicating the basis for our beliefs to the next generation. We need more theology. That doesn’t necessarily mean we need our kids reading thousand-page systematic theologies and listening to formal lectures. We need to put the cookies on the bottom shelf. That’s what the graphic novel adaptation of John Calvin’s Institutes of the Christian Religion does; it presents the core of Calvin’s doctrinal teaching in a visually engaging and intellectually stimulating format. I’ve generally been skeptical of graphic novels, but then I thought about how much I learned about philosophy from poring over Bill Watterson’s Calvin and Hobbes as a kid. This illustrated adaption of the Institutes can help introduce the next generation to the basics of Reformed theology. The series is a delightful reminder that theology is for everyone. 6. John Bunyan, adapted by Tyler Van Halteren, Christian’s Quest (Lithos Kids, 2026) There are many adaptations of Bunyan’s classic, The Pilgrim’s Progress . There’s good reason for that, since it’s been one of the best-selling Christian books in history. Important themes about the Christian life are illustrated well and are part of the Christian imaginary, but Bunyan’s archaic language makes it especially hard for young people to read. Van Halteren’s adapted prose, with Manuel Zepic’s illustrations, maintains the spirit of the original while making it

title: How to Fire Someone at a Christian Organization
summary: If managers do their jobs well, believe that God is sovereign, and bring the love of Christ even into hard conversations, everyone will be better off.
summary_zh: 无论是辅导经理、上游规划、接听电话、还是安排裁员。 每次都是艰难的。 与员工分离是经理最重的事情之一。 这样做既明确又友好,需要大量的准备和情绪调节.
title_zh: 如何在基督教组织中解雇某人
content: Over the course of my career, I’ve participated in more than 190 exits of employees, whether I was coaching a manager, planning upstream, sitting in on calls, or orchestrating layoffs. Each time was tough. Parting ways with an employee is one of the heaviest things a manager does. Doing it both clearly and kindly takes a lot of preparation and emotional regulation. In a faith-based workplace, these decisions can be even more surprising and hurtful, because managers try to spare the discomfort of a conversation about performance under any number of banners of being “kind.” How should we think about this as Christians who manage other Christians? Why Good Work Is Important A church’s mission is to spread the good news of Jesus, create ways for people to know him more deeply, and love our neighbors. A Christian nonprofit’s purpose is adjacent—to provide mercy, justice, evangelism, or discipleship while pointing people to Christ and their local church. This work happens through ministry and outreach staff, but also through effective operations. Doing this work takes all types of roles: pastors, administrators, and ministry coordinators; managers, accountants, and musicians; executive admins, facilities operators, and IT teams. Much of what it takes to run a church or Christian organization happens outside the hours of direct ministry. To do any of this well, churches and nonprofits must hire capable people who can effectively perform their duties and steward the mission. When managers in a secular workplace don’t hire wisely, I’ve seen the result in poor functional performance, departmental infighting, disengagement, acrimonious exits, and abuse of company resources. In a faith-based organization or church, you may get a mix of this and something worse: the spread of the gospel can be compromised too. Upstream Work for Managers As a manager, if you notice someone isn’t performing well, the best time to start talking about it isn’t at the exit conversation. It’s way upstream from that. Your core job is to ensure your people have what they need to be successful. That includes clear expectations, communication of what success looks like, feedback on performance, and accountability for meeting those standards. Ideally, you’re doing these on a regular basis in one-on-one meetings  and in performance check-ins throughout the year. Churches and nonprofits must hire capable people who can effectively perform their duties and steward the mission. This is a manager’s job, and faith-based organizations don’t have a softer standard. Where I’ve seen termination decisions and conversations go south—in Christian organizations or elsewhere—is when a manager doesn’t understand this. (Or, worse, they understand it but think that somehow it doesn’t apply to them.) Speaking to an employee about parting ways because you’ve consistently documented underperformance is a rough conversation. It’s far worse when your failure to give regular feedback leaves an employee blindsided, confused, and hurt when you need to broach termination. Often, that failure is rooted in a desire to avoid conflict or hurt feelings. The manager would rather spare himself the discomfort of a direct conversation. In a Christian organization, this impulse pulls hard. The employees under your care all love Jesus. They’re there to promote the church’s mission and spread the gospel. You may even sit shoulder to shoulder in the pews with them on Sundays. But James 4:17 has a word for managers who fail to do the difficult work: “Whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin.” Colossians 4:1 underlines this: “Masters, treat your bondservants justly and fairly, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven.” I’ve watched managers avoid the perceived sin of commission (telling someone he’s doing a poor job in his role) and step right into the sin of omission (letting the problem fester until the employee is struggling and a termination conversation seems inevitable). It doesn’t have to be this way. The hard thing and the loving thing aren’t at odds here. Justice, Mercy, and God’s Sovereignty at Work Let’s say you have an employee you’ve been coaching and providing with direct feedback about his (or her) performance. You’ve clearly communicated his responsibilities, warned him when he’s failed, given chances for improvement, and clarified what good performance looks like. It’s not a situation of grave moral failure or breach of ethics, just run-of-the-mill underperformance. What if he doesn’t improve? Are churches or Christian organizations allowed to fire someone for something besides moral failure? Is it fair to let someone go because he isn’t good at his church job? The short answer: Yes. Faith-based organizations hire people to perform a set of roles and responsibilities that contribute to the thriving of that organization. This means doing the job satisfactorily, abiding by the organization’s codes of conduct, and operating within legal bounds of employment. When someone—regardless of his intentions—fails to consistently meet these expectations, parting ways is a course of action that’s on the table. That’s not callous; it’s a means to preserve the integrity of the organization’s mission. But letting someone go should be a last resort . Managers can and should be sensitive to giving clear direction and expectations, continual feedback on what’s going well (or not), and a reasonable timeline to make improvements. And sometimes—for legal or other reasons—someone will need reasonable accommodations to get his work done. We need to give people as fair of a shot as possible to succeed. The worst situation for everyone is where a person is struggling, and the manager hasn’t done anything to intervene because a manager thinks his silent toleration is showing “mercy.” That behavior isn’t justice or mercy—it’s abdicating responsibility as a steward of your employees and your organization’s mission. But let’s say the manager has done his best to set clear expectations, addressed flagging performance, or provided reasonable accommodations. The employee still doesn’t seem to ever improve. What then? As managers, it’s easy to worry that termination ruins someone’s life. It’s tempting to want to avoid that conversation and to keep giving him chances to get better (even if he’s shown that’s not possible). But this can become a way to protect the manager from discomfort and a hard decision; it does nothing to benefit the employee. Silent toleration isn’t justice or mercy—it’s abdicating responsibility as a steward of your employees and your organization’s mission. When we hold back the hard call, we tell ourselves a story about mercy: I don’t want to be the one who upends this person’s life, so I won’t go there. That’s a heavy burden to put on your shoulders. To believe you’re ruining someone’s life by ending his employment is to believe you hold his future in your hands. But here’s the thing: You don’t. You aren’t sovereign over this person’s story. You cannot see his next chapter. The assumption that you can, that keeping him in a role where he’s failing is protecting him from some fate only you can foresee, isn’t humility. It’s pride. We’re obligated to be fair and right and just to the employees in our care (Prov. 2:9, 21:15; Mic. 6:8). Sometimes that means the consequences of one person’s poor behavior at work have to be addressed through parting ways. Remember that God also sees our work, and in his grace he often allows us to suffer the just consequences of our actions. We likewise need to be fair in managing performance even if that involves a hard call. Sometimes, letting a person go who isn’t performing is a boon to him long-term. It can be the catalyst to propel him to a future role or career where his abilities are better fit for what another organization needs. That’s hard to imagine when you’re in the thick of the situation, but from someone who has seen this play out scores of ti

title: Modernity Is Seeking a Hypergood. It’s Making Us Miserable.
summary: Why does modernity feel unlivable? Because secularism has its own versions of monotheism and polytheism.
summary_zh: 查尔斯·泰勒(Charles Taylor)在其著作"自我的来源"(Source of the Self)中认为,道德框架是多种多样的,是不可避免的. 没有一个中立的人能从距离和客观的角度, 来调查其他人的道德框架, 以及他们的偏见, 似乎不受自己道德框架的影响。 我们都有 从生命的开始,我们便开始适应特定的道德框架。 通过它们,我们构建了我们的身份,作为本身是道德空间的叙述。
title_zh: 现代性正在追求一种超善。它让我们痛苦不堪。
content: In his book Sources of the Self , Charles Taylor argues that moral frameworks are diverse and inescapable. There’s no neutral human being who can survey everyone else’s moral frameworks, with all their biases, from a position of distance and objectivity, as though untouched by a moral framework of his own. We all have them. From the beginning of life, we intuit particular moral frameworks. Through them, we construct our identities as narratives that are themselves moral spaces. Alongside this, as modern Western people, we treat the sense of self as a moral source in its own right. Whereas some cultures imagine esteem and validation to come from other people on the basis of our deeds (“You are a good person because you did . . .”), Western culture gives us a mantra of unconditional self-affirmation (“I am a good person because I say so”) even when the content our lives suggests otherwise. How should Christians in the West think about that local moral framework? In an important sense, it shows us we aren’t the only ones who think about our lives in terms of justification and sanctification. Rather, our secular neighbors live within secularized versions of those categories . Their sense of self makes a qualitative judgment that while life contains many goods, one good must rank highest. Alignment with that highest good is a powerful thing. It confers a justifying power on me, grounding my identity in something good. Having identified myself with that good, though, a hard and personal question necessarily follows: How does my actual life shape up with that highest good? In a secularized sense, Western culture teaches us to assess our “sanctification” in view of our “justification.” This framework makes sense of Taylor’s claim that all modern people are invested in counterparts to these deeply Christian notions. Beyond this, it also raises a prior question: How do modern Westernized people arrive at a highest good in the first place? Without a highest good, you have no standard by which to lay hold of justification or to measure your sanctification. Taylor’s work offers several lenses for answering that question, much like the lenses an optometrist combines in a refraction machine to produce a sharp image. Let’s focus on one of them: Taylor’s idea of the hypergood. The modern self arrives at its highest good by taking a finite, ordinary good and asking it to play the role of an ultimate one. Read alongside Augustine’s distinction between use and enjoyment , Taylor’s concept reveals this move as a form of idolatry. It overburdens the goods we elevate, damages the goods we neglect, and sets us in conflict with others and with ourselves. Only when the ultimate place belongs to God can ordinary goods be freed to be what they are. Why the ‘Good Life’ Is Hard to Define In chapter 3 of Sources of the Self , “Ethics of Inarticulacy,” Taylor argues that modern Western people find the concept of the “good life” difficult to grasp, for several reasons. Our identities have many layers that feed into and out of one another in ways that are hard to put into words. We recognize some of those layers as universal, such as abstract political or ideological commitments that also form the others people’s identities. We recognize other layers as highly particular to ourselves. I might share the same political label as you do, but you didn’t grow up in my town, in my family, or in my skin, and your experiences aren’t my experiences. Holding those two things together is an exceptionally burdensome task. The modern self arrives at its highest good by taking a finite, ordinary good and asking it to play the role of an ultimate one. Our present-day identities are also shaped by long and complex historical developments we struggle to narrate, or about which we are simply oblivious. Imagine being asked “What does it mean for you to be a British Christian?” and beginning your answer with “Well, around the year AD 600, Aethelberht, pagan king of Kent, converted to Christianity . . .” A year of solid talking later, you finally arrive at your life in 2026. Or imagine not even beginning with Aethelberht but with the words “Let us begin with the Homeric man.” That isn’t what we tend to do. Taylor identifies another factor in the ethics of inarticulacy, one he develops more fully in A Secular Age : the difference between living in a transcendent frame and living in an immanent frame. Sources of the Self represents a preparatory stage for that distinction, but the distinction is already emerging there. Consider a pre-Enlightenment, pre-Cartesian, premodern person, such as a medieval European. He experiences his sense of self in such a way that he believes his mind conforms to things, rather than things conforming to his mind. His moral framework intuits that all things are imbued with inherent meaning and sacred order and that the cosmos as a whole exists in relation to an order that exceeds it. This is life within a transcendent frame. It orients life around a proper distinction between many things that are relative and the one thing that is ontologically ultimate. The ultimate is categorically different from ordinary, nonultimate things. In Christian terms, this expresses the distinction between the Creator and the creature: One is ultimate, and the other is relative. In A Secular Age , Taylor traces the shift from medieval to modern as a shift from life in a transcendent frame to life in an immanent frame. In an immanent frame, things conform to my mind, and my sense of self is fundamentally buffered from my body, from my physical environment, and from any claims of metaphysical reality. The way I distinguish ultimate things from ordinary things is transformed as well, because the ultimate is no longer transcendent. It’s immanent. The ultimate as a categorically other, transcendent reality is gone. What happens instead is that I take something from the immanent realm, from the things near to me, and make it act as my ultimate thing. Taylor sees this as inescapable for the modern self: We all have something that takes ultimate place. He uses the language of “the thing you’d be at sea without.” If this thing weren’t holding my identity together, I couldn’t be me. I would be lost. The central question, then, is how does the modern secularized self, which Taylor elsewhere calls the buffered self in an immanent frame, arrive at a highest good? Taylor gives us a particularly useful lens. Taylor and the Hypergood Taylor introduces the idea of the hypergood in chapter 3 of Sources of the Self and continues to develop it in chapter 4, “Moral Sources.” Two caveats are in order. First, the hypergood appears only in Sources of the Self . Taylor doesn’t reprise it in subsequent works. Second, scholars of Taylor’s works have read the concept in different ways. Charles Blattberg, for instance, argues that hypergood is an underdeveloped concept within the book. My own reading is far closer to that of the Dutch philosopher Jasper van Buuren . The idea works like this: Everyone lives within a moral framework, however much we struggle to articulate it, and nobody lives within a moral framework free of value judgments. No one is an absolute relativist who finds every good to be equally important, because life isn’t livable that way. Life requires us to find some things more important than others. Without that, we would be completely overwhelmed and paralyzed by the multiplicity of the world. Our sense of agency would end, and we would become entirely passive, acted on but unable to act. In practice, modern people don’t generally live like this. Taylor describes how modern people often hold a hierarchy of increasingly important goods. For some, the high-ranking goods will be the ideal of rational self-mastery, family life, self-expression, or fame. He writes, Most of us not only live with many goods but find that we have to rank them, and in some cases, this ranking makes one of them of supreme importance
content_zh:
查尔斯·泰勒(Charles Taylor)在其著作"自我的来源"(Source of the Self)中认为,道德框架是多种多样的,是不可避免的. 没有一个中立的人能从距离和客观的角度, 来调查其他人的道德框架, 以及他们的偏见, 似乎不受自己道德框架的影响。 我们都有 从生命的开始,我们便开始适应特定的道德框架。
通过它们,我们构建了我们的身份,作为本身是道德空间的叙述。 与此同时,我们作为现代的西方人,将自我感作为道德来源。 虽然有些文化认为尊敬和认可来自他人,
西方文化给了我们一个无条件自我肯定的口号(“我是一个好人,因为我这样说”),即使我们的生活内容表明并非如此。 西方基督徒应该如何思考这个当地道德框架? 从重要的意义上讲,它向我们展示了我们并非唯一一个在理性和神圣化方面思考我们生活的人。
相反,我们的世俗邻居生活在这些类别的世俗版本中。 他们的自我意识做出了质的判断:虽然生活包含着许多商品,但一件好事必须排到最高. 与最高利益一致是一件很强大的事情。 它赋予我一个正当的权力, 将我的身份建立在一件好事上。
然而,我认同了这一点,因此,一个困难而个人的问题必然如下: 我真正的生命是如何 与最高的好?
从世俗化的意义上讲,西方文化教我们根据我们的“合理性”来评估我们的“安全性”。 这一框架说明了泰勒的说法,即所有现代人都投资于与这些虔诚的基督教观念相对应的人。 除此之外,它还提出了前一个问题: 现代被西方化的人是如何在第一时间到达最高的好?
没有最高的善,你没有标准 来证明你的理由或衡量你的圣洁。 Taylor的作品为回答这个问题提供了多张镜头,很像一个选取者在折射机中组合出一副尖锐的图像. 让我们关注其中之一:泰勒关于超好的想法。
只有当终极之地属于上帝时,普通的商品才能被释放出来,成为他们所应有的. “美好生活”为什么很难在“自我来源”第3章“Inarticulacy的道德”中定义,泰勒认为,现代西方人认为“美好生活”的概念很难理解,原因有几个。
我们的身份有许多层层,以难以言出必行的方式相互交流。 我们认识到,这些层次中有些是普遍性的,例如抽象的政治或意识形态承诺,它们也构成了其他人民的特性。 我们认识到,其他层面对我们自己来说是极为特殊的。
我们目前的身份也由我们努力叙述的长期而复杂的历史事态发展所决定,或者我们完全忽视这些事态发展。 想象一下被问到“你成为一位英国基督徒意味着什么?” 然后用“大约在AD 600年左右,肯特的异教国王Aethelberht皈依基督教......”开始回答。
你终于在2026年来到你的生活。 或者想象一下不要从Aethelberht开始, 这不是我们常做的。
Taylor确定了无艺术性伦理学的另一个因素,一个他在"世俗时代"中发展得更充分的因素:生活在超越性框架与活在永恒框架之间的区别. 自我来源是这种区别的准备阶段,但这种区别已经在那里出现。
考虑一个启蒙前,喀特斯前人,前现代人,如中世纪的欧洲人. 他以这样的方式体验了自己的自觉,以至于他认为他的思想符合事物,而不是符合他的思想. 他的道德框架因地制宜地认为,一切事物都充满了固有的意义和神圣的秩序,而宇宙整体存在于一个超越它的命令上.
这是在超乎寻常的框架内生活 它引导生命 围绕一个适当的区分 许多东西是相对的 和一件事 是本体论的终极。 终极绝对不同于平凡的,非终极的事物. 在基督教中,这表达了造物主和生物之间的区别: 一是终相相相相相相相相相相相相相相相相相相相相.
在"世俗时代"(A Secular Age)中,泰勒将从中世纪到现代的转变追溯为从超越性框架的生活到永生的转变. 在一个无穷无尽的框架里,事物符合我的思想,我的自我感从根本上从我的身体,从我的物理环境,以及任何对元物理现实的宣称中缓冲.
我区分最终事物和普通事物的方式也发生了转变,因为最终事物不再具有超越性. 这实在是一成不变。 终极作为另一个绝对超凡的现实已经消失. 相反的,我从永恒的王国, 从我身边的东西, 把它当作我的终极事物。
泰勒认为这对现代人来说是不可回避的:我们都有终极成就。 他使用“你在海上没有的东西”的语言。 如果这东西不把我的身份放在一起, 我会迷路的。
那么,核心问题是,现代世俗化的自我—— 泰勒在别处称之为在一成不变的框架中被缓冲的自我—— 如何达到最高的善? 泰勒给我们一个特别有用的镜头。 Taylor和Hypergood Taylor在《自我来源》第3章中提出了“自我来源”的概念,并在第4章“道德来源”中继续加以发展。 有两点需要注意。
首先,超好品只出现在Self源中。 泰勒在后来的作品中并没有重现它. 第二,泰勒作品的学者们以不同的方式解读了这一概念. 例如,查尔斯·布拉特伯格(Charles Blattberg)认为"超古德"是书中一个不发达的概念. 我本人的解读更接近荷兰哲学家贾斯珀·范·布伦的解读。
这个想法是这样运作的:每个人都生活在道德框架内,无论我们为阐明这个概念付出了多少努力,没有人生活在没有价值判断的道德框架内。 没有人是绝对的相对主义者, 生活需要我们找到一些比其他更重要的东西.
没有这些,我们将完全被世界的多面性所压倒和瘫痪。 我们的代理意识将结束,我们将完全被动地采取行动,但却无法采取行动。 现代人一般不会这样生活。 泰勒描述了现代人如何常常持有日益重要商品的等级.
对一些人来说,高级商品将是理性自管,家庭生活,自我表达,或名声的理想. 他写道,我们大多数人不仅生活 与很多商品, 发现我们必须排序, 在某些情况下,这种排名 使其中之一 至高无上

title: 40 Great Films for Christian Parents to Watch With Their Kids
summary: These excellent movies are enjoyable for families to watch together, but they’re also rich with values Christian parents can get behind.
summary_zh: 基督教家庭应该担心那些被称为“爱孩子”但却以精神上不健康的方式组建孩子的无数选择。 作为四个孩子的爸爸,我对斗争很了解 无法跟上向孩子们推销新电影和电视节目的内容传送带。 基督教家长需要值得信赖的馆长, 他们可以可靠地引导我们去娱乐, 这份名单是我在这场斗争中帮助基督教同胞父母的尝试. 下面的电影都是G级或PG级的,一般是“整个家庭的安全”,尽管父母仍应查阅在线内容指南,以了解他们特定家庭是否合适。
title_zh: 适合基督徒父母与孩子一起观看的40部优秀电影
content: In today’s glutted, morally compromised streaming-media environment, Christian families are right to worry about the countless options billed as “kid-friendly” but actually form kids in spiritually unhealthy ways. As a dad of four young kids, I know the struggle well. It’s impossible to keep up with the content conveyor belt of new film and TV options being marketed to kids. Christian parents need trusted curators who can reliably point us to entertainment that isn’t just “safe” for our kids to watch but is actively promoting laudable themes and (sometimes accidentally) modeling Christian virtue. This list is my attempt to help my fellow Christian parents in this struggle. The movies below are all G- or PG-rated and generally “safe for the whole family,” though parents should still consult online content guides to discern the appropriateness for their particular family. But the films I selected go beyond just safe . I commend them not only for what they don’t depict but for what they do. These movies are fun, well-made, and enjoyable for families to watch together ; they’re also rich with values Christian parents can get behind. These movies are rich with values Christian parents can get behind. I divided the list into two halves for different age groups: 20 films that might be better for your younger kids (9 and younger), and 20 films perhaps more appropriate for older kids (10 and older). If you have school-age kids, consider working your way through this list—making time not just to watch the movie together but also to discuss it afterward. Try to tease out the values and virtues the films celebrate. Cultivate in your kids a way of watching media wisely that might just become intuitive for them, with enough practice. To Watch with Younger Kids (9 and Younger) Beauty and the Beast (1991). For my money, this is the greatest of the great movies from the Disney animation heyday. The songs, the artistry, the themes of beauty, sacrifice, and love’s power to transform . . . the whole package is elegant and stately, with little of the “follow your heart” expressive individualism that compromises other Disney films of the era. Rated G. Cinderella (1950). Another all-time great Disney animated movie, the 1950 Cinderella is a gorgeous classic full of theological resonance. At a time when fairy tales and traditional romances are ridiculed or “modernized” in ways that blur moral lines, kids need the old stories where chivalric love is embraced and “happily ever after” endings aren’t pitched as problematic. Rated G. Coyote vs. Acme (2026). The newest release on this list, Coyote vs. Acme is one of the most enjoyable animated movies I’ve seen in years. Parents will laugh out loud at the satire and constant nostalgic callbacks, and kids will enjoy the vintage Looney Tunes physical humor. But more than just popcorn fun, this movie also celebrates unlikely friendship and perseverance in fighting for justice. Rated PG. David (2025). With animation as beautiful as any Disney or Pixar movie, this Angel Studios production about the biblical David blew my expectations away and landed on my top 10 list in 2025 . Biblically faithful and artistically excellent (the songs are catchy!), David has become a staple in our family’s rewatchable-movie diet. Rated PG. Despicable Me (2010). The Despicable Me franchise is one of my family’s favorites, and the first installment is rife with redemptive themes Christians can applaud. It’s the story of a hardened supervillain Gru (Steve Carell) who is morally transformed through the process of adopting three orphaned girls. Instead of the “good guy turns bad” trope that’s everywhere in pop culture, this is a “bad guy becomes better” story. Refreshing. Rated PG. Finding Nemo (2003). This is peak Pixar on both a storytelling and thematic level. The undersea adventure is visually stunning. But the film’s thematic explorations and insights for parenting are even richer. It’s a celebration of a father’s love for his son—which sometimes looks like zealous protectiveness and sometimes like letting kids learn lessons in freedom. Rated G. Homeward Bound: The Incredible Journey (1993). This lovable movie, about two dogs and a cat who band together to find their way home, was a staple of my childhood—and still holds up. It’s a classic hero’s journey, highly entertaining but also full of good lessons about perseverance, loyalty, family, and maturity. Rated G. How to Train Your Dragon (2010). This DreamWorks Animation triumph (recently remade as a “live-action” film) tells a fun story of a Viking boy who befriends and tames what should be his sworn enemy: a dragon. It’s a movie about the power of friendship to overcome fear. Rated PG. The Incredibles (2004). Brad Bird’s animated family superhero movie is one of several standouts from the golden age of Pixar (roughly 2001–2010) that made this list. I love how the movie celebrates the nuclear family, showing how a healthy, loving family unit becomes its own “superpower” greater than the sum of its parts. Rated PG. The Lion King (1994). I showed this movie to my kids for the first time recently, and they were utterly compelled. A generation after its release, The Lion King holds up as one of Disney’s 1990s animated masterpieces. The story is Shakespearean in scope and full of lessons in fortitude, justice, and choosing costly duty over carefree comfort. Rated G. Mary Poppins (1964) and Mary Poppins Returns (2018). The original Mary Poppins (starring Julie Andrews) and the recent sequel (starring Emily Blunt) are both immensely entertaining. They are also family-friendly and generally family- affirming musicals (aside from Mrs. Banks singing about how men are stupid). Arguably the original film represents a subversive critique of modernity . If your family hasn’t yet watched these classics together, make this duo a holiday-season double feature. Rated G and PG. The Muppet Christmas Carol (1992). Charles Dickens’s 1843 novella has been adapted many times, but the Muppet version is arguably the best. Faithful to the moral lessons of Dickens’s story but also just a lot of fun, this holiday classic celebrates the generous spirit of Christmas in the most wonderful ways. Rated G. Paddington series (2014, 2017, 2024). Paddington is perhaps the greatest “trilogy” ever in the kids’ movie genre. These movies are funny, sweet, and full of good lessons about family, bravery, and doing the right thing. They’re also just joyful, aesthetically vibrant, and clever in ways that appeal to all ages. Rated PG. The Peanuts Movie (2015). More kids today should be watching Peanuts cartoons. I try to annually show my kids It’s the Great Pumpkin , Charlie Brown and A Charlie Brown Christmas (both are on Apple TV). The Peanuts Movie captures the vintage, wholesome feel of the 1960s classics. Rated G. Pinocchio (1940). This is one of Disney’s earliest, and still most beloved, animated classics. The fairy tale is whimsical, at times dark, but rife with theological allusions. Its central question—what does it mean to be “real boy”?—has never been timelier and provides an entry point for a conversation parents can have with kids about humanity in an age of robots. Rated G. The Prince of Egypt (1998). The Exodus story is inherently cinematic, and the DreamWorks Animation classic remains a stunner. The artistry of the animation is at times jaw-dropping, and the story ( while not perfect ) is largely faithful to the biblical source material. Rated PG. Swiss Family Robinson (1960). This is a great movie to watch for all families, but especially if you have young boys. As the classic Disney film depicts the adventures of the shipwrecked Robinson family, it celebrates resourcefulness, teamwork, chivalry, and manly strength channeled toward providing and protecting. They don’t make virtuous adventure movies like this anymore. Rated G. Toy Story 1, 2, 3, and 5 (1995, 1999, 2010, 2026). The Toy Story movies are varying degrees of excellent

基督教家长需要值得信赖的馆长, 他们可以可靠地引导我们去娱乐, 这份名单是我在这场斗争中帮助基督教同胞父母的尝试.

title: Why Christianity Explains Our Deepest Longings
summary: ‘Why Christianity Makes Sense’ offers a compelling argument that Christianity explains the condition of both the world and the human heart.
summary_zh: 在整个教会历史中,上帝一直唤起忠实的声音,向每一代人讲福音. 使徒保罗出行于许多已知的世界,在犹太会堂和公共场合传教. 在雅典,他把文化所问的问题作为宣示福音的平台. 类似地,奥古斯丁,安塞尔姆,布莱斯·帕斯卡尔,C.
title_zh: 为什么基督教能够解释我们最深切的渴望
content: Throughout church history, God has raised up faithful voices to speak the gospel to each generation. The apostle Paul traveled through much of the known world, preaching in synagogues and public settings. In Athens, he used the questions the culture was asking as a platform from which to proclaim the gospel. Similarly, Augustine, Anselm, Blaise Pascal, C. S. Lewis, Tim Keller, and many others helped readers see Christianity’s coherence amid the questions and assumptions of their times. Through his online ministry, Truth Unites , Gavin Ortlund fills that sort of role in our cultural moment. In Why Christianity Makes Sense: A Book About Jesus, the Mysteries of the World, and the Longings in Your Heart , Ortlund offers an accessible defense of the faith for readers unsure whether Christianity can withstand serious examination. It’s also a useful tool for discipling believers bombarded with hard questions about Christianity on the internet. Ortlund’s goal is to show “why it makes sense to be a Christian” (xiii). Ortlund’s particular strength is that he recognizes our questions aren’t merely intellectual. They arise from deeper longings for meaning, purpose, and transcendence. Unknown God In Athens, Paul thoughtfully noticed an altar established “to the unknown god” (Acts 17:23). He didn’t mock them for it. Every generation builds an altar of its own. Augustine called it the restless heart; Lewis called it Sehnsucht , the longing that joy itself cannot satisfy. Keller called the traces it leaves behind clues . Ortlund has a name for it: “the ache.” Ortlund doesn’t begin with a technical exposition of the ache but by showing it’s the desire behind every altar to every unknown god. He asks, “Are you genuinely curious about what life means—why you’re here, and what it’s all for?” (xi). The ache is the restless longing for the transcendent that we can’t put into words. Just as hunger implies we live in a world where food is meant to fuel our bodies, so the desire for meaning points to the existence of something that will satisfy that desire. So many counterfeits promise to satisfy our desire for God. Many people have learned to deny any sense of longing for the divine or simply scroll past the question before it finishes loading in their minds. Just as hunger implies we live in a world where food is meant to fuel our bodies, so the desire for meaning points to the existence of something that will satisfy that desire. In a culture where the most shocking content on social media becomes boring, it’s worth drawing attention to Jesus’s radical claims. “He claimed to be the way, the truth, and the life,” notes Ortlund. “Muhammad taught the five pillars, Buddha spoke of enlightenment, Confucius pointed to the Way, but Jesus pointed to himself as the answer. In fact, Jesus claimed to be God” (104). The claim is preposterous, unless it’s true. So Ortlund asks his readers to put on their thinking caps: “What if God is real, and Jesus is this God, showing up in history to reveal himself to us? Why not? Is it really all that much crazier than the alternatives?” (104). It’s not. And more importantly, the solution Jesus offers is the most complete answer to the ache. This message deserves to be proclaimed in public. In the Marketplace When Paul was in Athens, he “reasoned . . . in the marketplace” (Acts 17:17), the agora, which is where ideas were exchanged. Our modern agora is increasingly virtual, less of a town square and more like the comment section of a microvlog. Ortlund has excelled in this space, making hard things plain in his videos without making them small. His talent for public communication comes through in this book. For example, Ortlund tackles divine hiddenness: Have you ever wondered why, if God is indeed real, his existence isn’t completely obvious? Why are religious matters so ambiguous ? Wouldn’t a loving God want to make things clear to us? (176) It’s an intuitive argument that undermines the sense that the ache is a longing that can be fulfilled by God. There are people who have really been yearning for truth whose “years of unanswered prayers have stacked up” (177). It can be hard to explain why their search hasn’t been more fruitful. Yet we don’t have to invent answers on our own. Ortlund draws from historical sources like Pascal to argue that “partial revelation of God is a necessary feature of Christian theology.” Ortlund continues, “This is the drama of the gospel: A God who sneaks into his creation as one person within it, but who came in a manger amidst the donkeys rather than with fanfare and trumpets” (178). God has given us enough evidence of his existence; we just don’t always believe it. Our biggest problem isn’t ignorance; it’s sin. So even if everything that could be known about God was as plain as day, we might still hate him in our pride. Thus, Ortlund concludes, “A true relationship with God requires humility, which is better served by diligent searching in a partial revelation” (184). Hiddenness, with the Christian God, is an invitation to be found. Ortlund’s gift is making this complex argument clear and compelling in a few pages that a teenager can read on his phone. Some Believed Paul had to preach in Athens because his audience had never heard of the gospel. After he told the crowd about Jesus’s resurrection, some mocked, some asked to hear more, but some believed. Our biggest problem isn’t ignorance; it’s sin. Our job isn’t to make people believe but to present the truth to them in an intelligible way. Ortlund shows Christians how to do that in Why Christianity Makes Sense , which is a reader-accessible highlight reel of his more academically geared book, Why God Makes Sense in a World That Doesn’t . This book is an ideal resource to put in the hands of a college student, away from home and all that’s familiar. It will help people seeking God to know him better—or maybe for the first time. The reflection questions at the end of each chapter make it suitable for personal study or within a small-group environment. Why Christianity Makes Sense offers a compelling argument that Christianity explains the condition of both the world and the human heart.

在整个教会历史中,上帝一直唤起忠实的声音,向每一代人讲福音. 使徒保罗出行于许多已知的世界,在犹太会堂和公共场合传教. 在雅典,他把文化所问的问题作为宣示福音的平台. 类似地,奥古斯丁,安塞尔姆,布莱斯·帕斯卡尔,C. S.
刘易斯,蒂姆·凯勒(Tim Keller)和其他许多人帮助读者在其时代的问题和假设中看到了基督教的一致性. Gavin Ortlund通过他的网络部,
Ortlund为读者提供信仰的可及辩护, 也是一种有用的工具,
Ortlund的目标是显示“为什么成为基督徒是有意义的”(十三)。 Ortlund的特长在于他承认我们的问题不仅仅是知识。 它们产生于对意义、目的和超越的更深的渴望。 在雅典,不知名之神,保罗深思熟虑地注意到一个“对不知名之神”设立的祭坛(第17:23号法案)。 他并没有嘲笑他们。
每代自建坛. 奥古斯丁称它为"不安的心";刘易斯称它为"Sehnsucht",即欢乐本身无法满足的渴望. Keller把留下的线索称为"线索" Ortlund有一个名字:“痛”。 Ortlund并不是从对痛的技术性阐述开始,
他问道,“你是否真的好奇生活的意义, 我们无法言出必行。 正如饥饿意味着我们生活在一个粮食意在为我们的身体提供燃料的世界中一样,因此,对含义的渴望表明存在能够满足这种愿望的东西。
这么多假货承诺满足我们对上帝的渴望. 许多人已经学会否认任何对神的渴望感,或者简单地在问题完成后将问题卷过一卷而来,在他们脑海中注入。 正如饥饿意味着我们生活在一个粮食意在为我们的身体提供燃料的世界中一样,因此,对含义的渴望表明存在能够满足这种愿望的东西。
在社交媒体上最令人震惊的内容变得无聊的文化中, “他声称自己是道路、真理和生命。” “穆罕默德教了五柱子,佛说开悟,孔子指道,但耶稣指道自取. 事实上,耶稣自称是上帝"(104).
除非是真的, 所以,奥尔特伦德要求他的读者戴上他们的思维盖子:"如果上帝是真实的,而耶稣是这个上帝,在历史上出现来向我们暴露自己呢? 为什么不呢? 这是否真的比其他选择更疯狂?”(104)。 事实并非如此。 更重要的是,耶稣给出的解决方案是对痛楚最完整的答案.
这一信息应当公开发表。 在市场上,保罗在雅典时,他“在市场上为......辩护”(第17:17号法),即交换思想的地方。 更像是微相机的评论部分。
Ortlund在这个空间里表现得非常出色, 他的公开交流天赋在本书中通过. 例如,Ortlund处理神圣的隐性: 如果上帝是真的, 为什么他的存在并不完全明显? 为什么宗教事务如此模糊? 爱的上帝难道不想让我们明白吗?
(176) 这是一种直觉性的论点,它破坏了痛感是上帝能够实现的渴望。 有些人真正渴望的是真理,他们“多年的未经答复的祈祷已经堆积起来”(177年)。 很难解释为何他们的搜寻没有取得更大的成果。 但我们不必独自发明答案。
Ortlund从帕斯卡这样的历史渊源中引申出“部分启示上帝是基督教神学的一个必要特征。” Ortlund继续说,“这是福音的剧情:一个潜入他作为其中一人而创造的上帝,但他却在驴子中走来,而不是用扇子和小号来跑来”(178)。 上帝为我们提供了他存在的充分证据;
我们并不总是相信这一点。 我们最大的问题不是无知,而是罪恶。 所以,即使一切可以知道 关于上帝的 和白天一样平淡, 我们可能仍然恨他 我们的骄傲。 因此,Ortlund最后说,“与上帝的真正关系需要谦卑,如果在部分启示中勤奋地寻找,则会更好”(184)。
隐藏,与基督教神一起,是一个被找到的邀请. Ortlund的天赋在几页中使这个复杂的论点清晰而令人信服, 一些人相信保罗不得不去雅典传教,因为他的观众从未听说过福音. 他告诉了群众耶稣复活的消息后,有些人嘲笑了,有些人要求听到更多,但有些人相信.
我们最大的问题不是无知,而是罪恶。 我们的工作不是让人们相信, Ortlund 向基督徒展示如何在《基督教如何创造理智》中做到这一点,
这本书是一个理想的资源, 这将帮助人们寻求上帝,以便更了解他,或许是第一次。 每章结尾的反射问题使其适合个人学习或在小群体环境中学习.
为什么基督教让理智提出令人信服的论点,认为基督教解释世界状况和人心。

title: Using Exercise to Help Us Through the Dark Times (with Lindsey Bomgren)
summary: Fitness can be a vain, selfie-driven world. Lindsey Bomgren, founder of Nourish Move Love, shares how she found her calling there: helping women get ‘strong for their tasks’ through difficult seasons and circumstances.
summary_zh: 在"世界之角"一集中,丹·多里安尼和马克·弗罗戈普(Mark Vroegop)与"努里什移动之恋"(Nourish Move Love)的创始人林西·博姆格伦(Lindsey Bomgren)交谈,这是一家以明尼阿波利斯为基地的健身企业,花了11年时间帮助女性在家中获得力量. 一位前大学生运动员和三位母亲Lindsey在网络上打造了一个排名最高的产后锻炼计划, 她与上帝摔跤多年, Lindsey解释为什么基督徒不应该把身体当成事后思考, 她讲述了Nourish Move Love这个名字背后的故事, 要有计划,记住10分钟比零好,而贸易外观目标则是进步目标。
title_zh: 通过运动帮助我们度过黑暗时期（与Lindsey Bomgren）
content: In this episode of Your Corner of the World , Dan Doriani and Mark Vroegop talk with Lindsey Bomgren, founder of Nourish Move Love , a Minneapolis-based fitness business that has spent 11 years helping women get strong at home. A former college athlete and a mother of three, Lindsey built one of the internet’s top-ranked postpartum workout programs, and she wrestled with God for years over whether a career in fitness could serve anyone at all. Lindsey explains why Christians shouldn’t treat their bodies as an afterthought, drawing on Proverbs 31 (“Her arms are strong for her tasks,” NIV), Paul’s words on physical training and godliness, and the parable of the talents. She tells the story behind the name Nourish Move Love, opens up about a dark postpartum season that gave her new empathy for struggling women, and offers practical encouragement for beginners: Have a plan, remember that 10 minutes is better than zero, and trade appearance-based goals for progress-based ones. She also describes the long grind of building a business by giving her content away, and the burnout that led her to rethink it. Resources Mentioned: Blue Ocean Strategy by W. Chan Kim and Renée Mauborgne The Body Teaches the Soul by Justin Whitmel Earley Habits of the Household by Justin Whitmel Earley
